Electrical Pop Quizzes
Practice Material - 16 Courses • 71 Modules



      16 quizzes, one per course. 10 multiple-choice questions per quiz - 160 questions in total.

      Answer key separate: No answers follow each quiz. Print pages 2-33 for the quizzes only. The
      Answer Key is in a separate section at the back, grouped Quiz 1 through Quiz 16.

      How to use: Complete one quiz at a time. Score it from the key at the back. Target 9/10 before
      moving on. Record your retake date and second score in the Answer Key section.

Quiz 1 - Mastering Electric Principles
Name: ________________________________ Date: ________________ Score: ___ / 10

   Modules Covered (6): Electronic Theory • Conductivity and Ohm's Laws • Understanding Electrical Principles Water
   Analogy • Practical Use of Ohm's Laws • Elements That Every Circuit Must Have • Understanding Circuit Protection Series
   and Partial Circuits



1. In conventional current flow theory, current is said to flow:
Module: Electronic Theory
    A. From negative to positive through the load
    B. From positive to negative through the external circuit
    C. Only inside the battery
    D. From ground directly to the load

2. An atom with electrons that move easily between atoms is best described as:
Module: Electronic Theory
    A. An insulator
    B. A semiconductor only when cold
    C. A conductor
    D. A capacitor

3. According to Ohm's Law, if voltage stays the same and resistance doubles, current will:
Module: Conductivity and Ohm's Laws
    A. Double
    B. Stay the same
    C. Fall to half
    D. Increase four times

4. A 12 V circuit has 4 ohms of resistance. How much current flows?
Module: Conductivity and Ohm's Laws
    A. 0.33 A
    B. 3 A
    C. 16 A
    D. 48 A

5. In the water analogy for electricity, water pressure is most like:
Module: Understanding Electrical Principles Water Analogy
    A. Resistance
    B. Current flow
    C. Voltage
    D. Capacitance




Electrical Pop Quizzes - Practice Material • Quiz 1 - Mastering Electric Principles • Page 2
Quiz 1 - Mastering Electric Principles (continued)

6. In the water analogy, a partly closed valve that restricts flow is most like:
Module: Understanding Electrical Principles Water Analogy
    A. A battery
    B. Resistance in the circuit
    C. A fuse
    D. Voltage drop only at the source

7. A bulb draws 2 A from a 12 V supply. Its resistance is:
Module: Practical Use of Ohm's Laws
    A. 24 ohms
    B. 10 ohms
    C. 6 ohms
    D. 0.17 ohms

8. A motor uses 120 W on a 12 V system. Approximately how much current does it draw?
Module: Practical Use of Ohm's Laws
    A. 0.1 A
    B. 10 A
    C. 12 A
    D. 1440 A

9. Which set lists elements every complete circuit must have?
Module: Elements That Every Circuit Must Have
    A. Source, protection, load and return path
    B. Only a battery and a switch
    C. Relay, sensor and module only
    D. Fuse, capacitor and resistor only

10. In a series circuit, if one load opens, what happens?
Module: Understanding Circuit Protection Series and Partial Circuits
    A. Other loads work brighter
    B. Current stops through the whole series path
    C. Voltage doubles at each load
    D. Resistance falls to zero

   Modules Covered (4): Fundamental Multimeter Functions • Measuring Amps and Volts and Resistance • Understanding
   Duty Cycles and PWM • Testing Diodes and Continuity



1. To measure voltage, the meter leads are connected:
Module: Fundamental Multimeter Functions
    A. In series with the load
    B. In parallel across the component or circuit
    C. With power off across a fuse only
    D. Red to ground only, black removed

2. Before measuring resistance on a component, you should:
Module: Fundamental Multimeter Functions
    A. Leave the circuit powered
    B. Disconnect power and isolate the component where needed
    C. Set the meter to amps
    D. Short the leads together permanently

3. To measure current with a standard multimeter, the meter is placed:
Module: Measuring Amps and Volts and Resistance
    A. In parallel with the load
    B. In series in the circuit
    C. Across the battery posts
    D. On the resistance scale

4. A meter on the 20 V DC scale reads 12.6 on a resting battery. This indicates:
Module: Measuring Amps and Volts and Resistance
    A. A discharged battery
    B. Approximately full charge at rest
    C. Overcharging
    D. An open cell in every case

5. When checking resistance, infinite or OL on the display most likely means:
Module: Measuring Amps and Volts and Resistance
    A. Zero resistance
    B. An open circuit or resistance beyond the range
    C. A short to ground
    D. Correct continuity




Electrical Pop Quizzes - Practice Material • Quiz 2 - Essential Multimeter Skills • Page 4
Quiz 2 - Essential Multimeter Skills (continued)

6. Duty cycle describes:
Module: Understanding Duty Cycles and PWM
    A. Battery voltage only
    B. The percentage of time a signal is on during one cycle
    C. The frequency in hertz only
    D. Resistance of a solenoid

7. A PWM solenoid at 75% duty cycle is:
Module: Understanding Duty Cycles and PWM
    A. On 25% of the time
    B. Off all the time
    C. On 75% of the time
    D. Operating only on AC

8. If frequency increases but duty cycle stays the same, what happens?
Module: Understanding Duty Cycles and PWM
    A. Each cycle gets shorter, but the on proportion stays the same
    B. Duty becomes voltage
    C. Current must fall to zero
    D. The signal becomes DC

9. In diode test mode, a good silicon diode tested in forward bias typically shows about:
Module: Testing Diodes and Continuity
    A. 0 V
    B. 0.5 to 0.7 V
    C. 12 V
    D. OL in both directions

10. A continuity beeper sounding does NOT by itself prove:
Module: Testing Diodes and Continuity
    A. The path has very high resistance
    B. The circuit can carry full load current without voltage drop
    C. The fuse is the correct rating
    D. The battery is charged

Quiz 3 - Advanced Multimeter Skills
Name: ________________________________ Date: ________________ Score: ___ / 10

   Modules Covered (2): Getting the Most From a Multimeter • Advanced Multimeter Functions



1. Using a meter's MIN/MAX recording is most useful for:
Module: Getting the Most From a Multimeter
    A. Polishing terminals
    B. Catching intermittent voltage drops or glitches over time
    C. Measuring tyre pressure
    D. Replacing a fuse rating

2. Why select a manual range instead of autoranging during a fast-changing test?
Module: Getting the Most From a Multimeter
    A. Autoranging always reads AC
    B. Manual range avoids range-hunting delays and unstable readings
    C. Manual range increases battery voltage
    D. It disables the leads

3. A low-impedance meter mode is preferred when checking for unwanted 'ghost' voltage because it:
Module: Getting the Most From a Multimeter
    A. Raises circuit voltage
    B. Loads the circuit slightly so induced voltage collapses
    C. Measures resistance with power on
    D. Disables continuity

4. Relative (REL) mode is used to:
Module: Getting the Most From a Multimeter
    A. Zero out lead resistance or a reference value
    B. Convert AC to DC
    C. Test diodes only
    D. Increase the fuse rating

5. When measuring a small parasitic draw, the best practice is to:
Module: Getting the Most From a Multimeter
    A. Open the circuit suddenly and lose module memory settings where avoidable
    B. Use an inductive clamp or a shunt method that keeps the circuit powered while modules sleep
    C. Rev the engine continuously
    D. Disconnect every module at once




Electrical Pop Quizzes - Practice Material • Quiz 3 - Advanced Multimeter Skills • Page 6
Quiz 3 - Advanced Multimeter Skills (continued)

6. A meter with True RMS is important when measuring:
Module: Advanced Multimeter Functions
    A. Only pure DC battery voltage
    B. Non-sinusoidal AC waveforms accurately
    C. Resistance of a bulb
    D. Continuity

7. Frequency measurement on a multimeter reports:
Module: Advanced Multimeter Functions
    A. Duty cycle only
    B. Cycles per second in hertz
    C. Voltage drop in millivolts
    D. Diode forward voltage

8. A bar graph on a digital meter helps the technician to:
Module: Advanced Multimeter Functions
    A. See rapid fluctuations that digits update too slowly to show
    B. Read tyre tread depth
    C. Charge the battery
    D. Decode CAN messages

9. Using a temperature probe with a multimeter is useful for:
Module: Advanced Multimeter Functions
    A. Checking a thermostat, radiator or connector for abnormal heating
    B. Setting ignition timing
    C. Measuring current directly
    D. Testing CAN resistance

10. Capacitance mode on a multimeter should be used:
Module: Advanced Multimeter Functions
    A. On a live 12 V circuit
    B. On a discharged, isolated capacitor
    C. While cranking only
    D. Instead of a scope for all waveforms

Quiz 4 - Diagnosing Circuit Faults
Name: ________________________________ Date: ________________ Score: ___ / 10

   Modules Covered (7): Open and Short Circuits • Terminal Tension and Back Probing • Wire Repair Best Practice •
   Locating Harness Faults • What is Voltage Drop • Signal Circuit Voltage Drop Checks • Using Voltage Drops as an
   Electrical Diagnostic Tool



1. A short to ground before the load will most likely:
Module: Open and Short Circuits
    A. Reduce voltage drop across the load to normal
    B. Blow the fuse or trip protection
    C. Make the load brighter
    D. Increase resistance in a controlled way

2. An open circuit is best defined as:
Module: Open and Short Circuits
    A. Too much current
    B. A break that stops current flow in the path
    C. A path to ground after the load
    D. Low resistance everywhere

3. Back probing a sealed connector is preferred to piercing insulation because it:
Module: Terminal Tension and Back Probing
    A. Damages the weather seal
    B. Avoids exposing copper to corrosion
    C. Increases terminal drag
    D. Bypasses the fuse

4. Poor terminal tension (drag) can cause:
Module: Terminal Tension and Back Probing
    A. Perfect signal transfer
    B. Intermittent opens and heat at the connection
    C. Higher fuel pressure
    D. A stronger ground

5. The preferred repair for a critical harness wire is generally:
Module: Wire Repair Best Practice
    A. Twist wires and tape only
    B. Solder or sealed crimp splice with heat-shrink, following manufacturer guidance
    C. Any household connector
    D. Leave strands cut if most remain




Electrical Pop Quizzes - Practice Material • Quiz 4 - Diagnosing Circuit Faults • Page 8
Quiz 4 - Diagnosing Circuit Faults (continued)
6. A wiggle test while monitoring a meter or scope helps to:
Module: Locating Harness Faults
    A. Set fuse ratings
    B. Reveal intermittent opens or shorts when the harness moves
    C. Charge a battery
    D. Measure tread wear

7. Voltage drop is:
Module: What is Voltage Drop
    A. Voltage used as current passes through resistance in a loaded circuit
    B. Battery voltage with everything off only
    C. Voltage created by a magnet
    D. The same as an open circuit voltage reading

8. Voltage drop testing must be done:
Module: What is Voltage Drop
    A. With the circuit off and disconnected
    B. With the circuit operating under load
    C. Only with an ohmmeter
    D. After removing the load

9. On a 5 V sensor signal circuit, an unwanted drop is most concerning because:
Module: Signal Circuit Voltage Drop Checks
    A. Signal circuits carry high starter current
    B. Small drops represent a large percentage error in the signal
    C. It only affects the ground side
    D. Modules ignore signal voltage

10. A ground side voltage drop of 0.8 V on a cranking circuit indicates:
Module: Using Voltage Drops as an Electrical Diagnostic Tool
    A. A perfect ground
    B. Excessive resistance in the ground path
    C. Low battery state of charge only
    D. A faulty starter relay rating

Quiz 5 - Wiring Harness Fundamentals

   Modules Covered (6): Automotive Cable Selection • Automotive Cable Size • Automotive Cable Crimping • DETSC
   Connectors • Understanding Automotive Soldering • Automotive Soldering Best Practice



1. When selecting replacement cable, the most important factors are:
Module: Automotive Cable Selection
    A. Colour only
    B. Current capacity, length, insulation and environment
    C. Price only
    D. Diameter of the connector shell only

2. A cable run near exhaust heat requires:
Module: Automotive Cable Selection
    A. Thinner insulation
    B. Insulation rated for the higher temperature
    C. No protection at all
    D. Household flex cable

3. If a circuit's cable is too thin for its length and current, the result is:
Module: Automotive Cable Size
    A. Less voltage drop
    B. Excessive voltage drop and heating
    C. Higher charging voltage
    D. No effect if the fuse is large

4. Doubling a cable's length, with the same gauge and current, will:
Module: Automotive Cable Size
    A. Halve its resistance
    B. Increase total resistance and voltage drop
    C. Remove voltage drop
    D. Increase fuse rating automatically

5. A correct crimp should:
Module: Automotive Cable Crimping
    A. Cut most strands for a tight fit
    B. Compress the terminal evenly, gripping conductor and insulation support without cutting strands
    C. Be loose enough to rotate
    D. Be covered without inspection




Electrical Pop Quizzes - Practice Material • Quiz 5 - Wiring Harness Fundamentals • Page 10
Quiz 5 - Wiring Harness Fundamentals (continued)

6. The pull test after crimping checks:
Module: Automotive Cable Crimping
    A. Insulation colour
    B. Mechanical strength of the crimp joint
    C. Battery voltage
    D. Fuse rating

7. A sealed automotive connector's weather seals are there to:
Module: DETSC Connectors
    A. Increase resistance
    B. Keep moisture and contamination out of the terminal area
    C. Make terminals looser
    D. Replace terminal locks

8. A terminal position assurance (TPA) lock does what?
Module: DETSC Connectors
    A. Raises system voltage
    B. Confirms and holds terminals fully seated in the housing
    C. Tests the circuit
    D. Acts as a fuse

9. In soldering, flux is used to:
Module: Understanding Automotive Soldering
    A. Insulate the finished joint permanently
    B. Clean oxides and help solder flow and wet the metals
    C. Cool the joint
    D. Increase resistance

10. A dull, grainy solder joint that moved while cooling is called a:
Module: Automotive Soldering Best Practice
    A. Cold / dry joint, and it should be remade
    B. Perfect joint
    C. Crimp joint
    D. Sealed joint

   Modules Covered (3): Automotive Relays • Circuit Relays • Monitored Relay Circuits



1. A relay allows:
Module: Automotive Relays
    A. A high-current circuit to be controlled by a low-current switch or module
    B. Voltage to be created without a source
    C. Resistance to disappear
    D. A fuse to be bypassed safely

2. On a typical ISO relay, terminals 85 and 86 are:
Module: Automotive Relays
    A. The load contacts
    B. The coil terminals
    C. Both grounds only
    D. The fuse terminals

3. On a typical 4-pin relay, terminal 30 is commonly:
Module: Automotive Relays
    A. Coil ground
    B. Common contact feed (power in)
    C. Signal ground
    D. Diode cathode only

4. When the coil is energised on a normally open relay, terminals 30 and 87:
Module: Automotive Relays
    A. Disconnect
    B. Connect, feeding the load
    C. Both go to ground
    D. Become the coil

5. A relay that clicks but the load does not work could have:
Module: Circuit Relays
    A. Only a good contact set
    B. Burnt or high-resistance contacts
    C. Too much terminal tension
    D. A charged battery in every case




Electrical Pop Quizzes - Practice Material • Quiz 6 - Automotive Relays Explained • Page 12
Quiz 6 - Automotive Relays Explained (continued)

6. Testing a relay circuit is best done by checking:
Module: Circuit Relays
    A. Coil feed, coil ground/control, contact feed and output under load
    B. Colour of the relay only
    C. Fuse rating only
    D. Battery brand

7. A suppression diode or resistor across a relay coil is used to:
Module: Circuit Relays
    A. Increase coil current sharply
    B. Control the voltage spike when the coil switches off
    C. Act as the load
    D. Replace the contacts

8. In a monitored relay circuit, the control module can detect a fault by:
Module: Monitored Relay Circuits
    A. Guessing
    B. Watching expected voltage/current feedback on the circuit
    C. Measuring tyre pressure
    D. Reading the relay colour

9. If a module commands a relay on but sees no voltage change on the monitor line, it will likely:
Module: Monitored Relay Circuits
    A. Ignore it forever
    B. Log a circuit fault
    C. Increase alternator output
    D. Disable the brakes

10. An open in a monitored relay's coil circuit would be detected as:
Module: Monitored Relay Circuits
    A. Normal operation
    B. No coil current / incorrect feedback when commanded
    C. High fuel trim
    D. Low oil pressure

   Modules Covered (5): Introduction to Automotive Lighting • Incandescent and Halogen Lighting Technology • High
   Intensity Discharge Lighting Technology • LED Lighting Technology • Laser Lighting Technology



1. A headlamp circuit fault causing one dim lamp most often points to:
Module: Introduction to Automotive Lighting
    A. High resistance or poor ground on that lamp's circuit
    B. Excess alternator voltage for all lamps
    C. Correct operation
    D. Low fuel level

2. Daytime running lights are intended to:
Module: Introduction to Automotive Lighting
    A. Replace headlamps at night
    B. Make the vehicle more visible during the day
    C. Increase battery drain as a test
    D. Signal braking

3. A halogen bulb should not be touched with bare fingers because:
Module: Incandescent and Halogen Lighting Technology
    A. Fingerprints change its colour
    B. Oils create hot spots that shorten bulb life
    C. It will not fit afterwards
    D. It becomes an LED

4. In an incandescent bulb, light is produced by:
Module: Incandescent and Halogen Lighting Technology
    A. A gas arc
    B. Heating a filament until it glows
    C. A laser diode
    D. A phosphor only

5. HID lamps produce light by:
Module: High Intensity Discharge Lighting Technology
    A. A heated filament
    B. An electric arc through xenon gas and metal salts
    C. A single LED chip
    D. Burning a wick




Electrical Pop Quizzes - Practice Material • Quiz 7 - Vehicle Lighting Technology • Page 14
Quiz 7 - Vehicle Lighting Technology (continued)

6. The ballast in an HID system is needed to:
Module: High Intensity Discharge Lighting Technology
    A. Lower voltage to 3 V only
    B. Provide high ignition voltage and then regulate lamp current
    C. Charge the battery
    D. Control the wipers

7. A key advantage of LED lighting is:
Module: LED Lighting Technology
    A. High heat at the lens in all designs
    B. Low current draw, long life and instant on
    C. It never needs a driver circuit
    D. It works with any voltage without control

8. If polarity is reversed to a standard LED lamp, it will typically:
Module: LED Lighting Technology
    A. Work brighter
    B. Not light, because LEDs allow current in one direction
    C. Become a halogen lamp
    D. Blow every fuse instantly in all cases

9. Laser headlights actually produce white light visible on the road by:
Module: Laser Lighting Technology
    A. Shining a raw blue laser directly with no conversion
    B. Using laser diodes to excite a phosphor that emits white light
    C. Burning fuel
    D. Reflecting sunlight only

10. Compared with LED, a main claimed benefit of laser high beam is:
Module: Laser Lighting Technology
    A. Lower cost in every vehicle
    B. Longer range from a very small, intense light source
    C. No electronics needed
    D. Wider use as brake lights

    B. Low at all times

6. An inductive (variable reluctance) crank sensor produces:

Answer Key
Separate Section - Do Not Print With the Quizzes



   This section begins after all 16 quizzes. Each quiz is grouped separately with the correct letter and
   a brief explanation for every question.

   After marking, record your retake date and second score on each quiz's key page. Target: 9/10
   before moving on.
Answer Key - Quiz 1 - Mastering Electric Principles
Retake date: ________________ Second score: ___ / 10

1. B - From positive to negative through the external circuit
    Conventional flow is described as positive to negative through the external circuit; electron flow is the opposite direction.

2. C - A conductor
    Conductors have free electrons that move easily, allowing current flow.

3. C - Fall to half
    I = V / R, so doubling R at fixed V halves current.

4. B - 3 A
    I = 12 / 4 = 3 A.

5. C - Voltage
    Pressure pushes water as voltage pushes charge through a circuit.

6. B - Resistance in the circuit
    Restriction to flow models resistance restricting current.

7. C - 6 ohms
    R = V / I = 12 / 2 = 6 ohms.

8. B - 10 A
    I = P / V = 120 / 12 = 10 A.

9. A - Source, protection, load and return path
    A working circuit needs a power source, protection, a load, conductors and a return path, usually with control.

10. B - Current stops through the whole series path
    A series path has one route for current, so an open stops current everywhere in that path.




Electrical Pop Quizzes - Answer Key • Quiz 1 - Mastering Electric Principles
Answer Key - Quiz 2 - Essential Multimeter Skills
Retake date: ________________ Second score: ___ / 10

1. B - In parallel across the component or circuit
    A voltmeter connects in parallel across the part being measured.

2. B - Disconnect power and isolate the component where needed
    Resistance is measured on an unpowered, preferably isolated component, or readings will be wrong and the meter may be
    damaged.

3. B - In series in the circuit
    Current measurement puts the meter in series so circuit current flows through it, within its rating.

4. B - Approximately full charge at rest
    About 12.6 V at rest is the expected fully charged lead-acid battery voltage.

5. B - An open circuit or resistance beyond the range
    OL means overload/open - no measurable continuity within the selected range.

6. B - The percentage of time a signal is on during one cycle
    Duty cycle is on-time as a percentage of the total cycle time.

7. C - On 75% of the time
    75% duty means energised for 75% of each cycle.

8. A - Each cycle gets shorter, but the on proportion stays the same
    Higher frequency shortens cycle time; the percentage on stays the same.

9. B - 0.5 to 0.7 V
    A silicon diode drops roughly 0.5-0.7 V when forward biased.

10. B - The circuit can carry full load current without voltage drop
    Continuity only shows a path exists; a single strand can beep yet drop voltage badly under load.




Electrical Pop Quizzes - Answer Key • Quiz 2 - Essential Multimeter Skills
Answer Key - Quiz 3 - Advanced Multimeter Skills
Retake date: ________________ Second score: ___ / 10

1. B - Catching intermittent voltage drops or glitches over time
   MIN/MAX captures the lowest and highest values seen during monitoring, helping find intermittents.

2. B - Manual range avoids range-hunting delays and unstable readings
   Fixing the range stops the meter hunting between ranges while the value changes quickly.

3. B - Loads the circuit slightly so induced voltage collapses
   Low impedance loads the circuit, so capacitively coupled ghost voltage disappears while real supply remains.

4. A - Zero out lead resistance or a reference value
   REL subtracts a reference, such as lead resistance, from later readings.

5. B - Use an inductive clamp or a shunt method that keeps the circuit powered while modules sleep
   Keeping the circuit intact with a clamp or shunt avoids waking modules and losing settings.

6. B - Non-sinusoidal AC waveforms accurately
   True RMS gives accurate AC readings on distorted or non-sine waveforms.

7. B - Cycles per second in hertz
   Frequency is measured in hertz, the number of cycles per second.

8. A - See rapid fluctuations that digits update too slowly to show
   The fast-updating bar graph shows trends and flicker the numeric display misses.

9. A - Checking a thermostat, radiator or connector for abnormal heating
   Temperature comparison finds restrictions, poor connections and cooling faults.

10. B - On a discharged, isolated capacitor
   Capacitors must be discharged and isolated before capacitance testing for safety and accuracy.




Electrical Pop Quizzes - Answer Key • Quiz 3 - Advanced Multimeter Skills
Answer Key - Quiz 4 - Diagnosing Circuit Faults
Retake date: ________________ Second score: ___ / 10

1. B - Blow the fuse or trip protection
   A pre-load short to ground creates excessive current, opening the fuse or protection.

2. B - A break that stops current flow in the path
   An open is a break in the path so current cannot flow.

3. B - Avoids exposing copper to corrosion
   Back probing tests the circuit without breaking insulation and inviting corrosion.

4. B - Intermittent opens and heat at the connection
   Loose terminals make poor contact, causing intermittents, voltage drop and heat.

5. B - Solder or sealed crimp splice with heat-shrink, following manufacturer guidance
   A sealed solder or crimp splice restores strength, conductivity and corrosion protection.

6. B - Reveal intermittent opens or shorts when the harness moves
   Moving the harness while watching readings exposes movement-sensitive faults.

7. A - Voltage used as current passes through resistance in a loaded circuit
   Voltage drop is the voltage consumed across resistance while current flows.

8. B - With the circuit operating under load
   No current means no meaningful voltage drop, so the circuit must be loaded and operating.

9. B - Small drops represent a large percentage error in the signal
   Low-current signal circuits need accuracy; even small unwanted drops distort sensor information.

10. B - Excessive resistance in the ground path
   A high ground drop under load points to resistance in cables, connections or ground points.




Electrical Pop Quizzes - Answer Key • Quiz 4 - Diagnosing Circuit Faults
Answer Key - Quiz 5 - Wiring Harness Fundamentals
Retake date: ________________ Second score: ___ / 10

1. B - Current capacity, length, insulation and environment
   Cable must carry the current over its length and suit heat, oil and abrasion conditions.

2. B - Insulation rated for the higher temperature
   Heat-rated insulation prevents melting, shorting and premature failure.

3. B - Excessive voltage drop and heating
   Undersized cable has more resistance, causing drop and heat under load.

4. B - Increase total resistance and voltage drop
   Longer conductors have more resistance, so drop increases.

5. B - Compress the terminal evenly, gripping conductor and insulation support without cutting strands
   A good crimp is gas-tight, mechanically strong and does not damage strands.

6. B - Mechanical strength of the crimp joint
   A gentle pull confirms the terminal is securely attached.

7. B - Keep moisture and contamination out of the terminal area
   Seals protect against water ingress and corrosion at the connection.

8. B - Confirms and holds terminals fully seated in the housing
   TPA secondary locks keep terminals from backing out.

9. B - Clean oxides and help solder flow and wet the metals
   Flux removes oxides so solder bonds properly to the conductors.

10. A - Cold / dry joint, and it should be remade
   Movement or insufficient heat makes a weak, high-resistance cold joint.




Electrical Pop Quizzes - Answer Key • Quiz 5 - Wiring Harness Fundamentals
Answer Key - Quiz 6 - Automotive Relays Explained
Retake date: ________________ Second score: ___ / 10

1. A - A high-current circuit to be controlled by a low-current switch or module
   The coil (low current) controls contacts that switch the high-current load circuit.

2. B - The coil terminals
   85 and 86 are the relay coil connections.

3. B - Common contact feed (power in)
   Terminal 30 is the common contact, usually the power feed to the contacts.

4. B - Connect, feeding the load
   Energising the coil closes 30 to 87 on a normally open relay.

5. B - Burnt or high-resistance contacts
   Clicking proves coil operation, not that the contacts carry current cleanly.

6. A - Coil feed, coil ground/control, contact feed and output under load
   All four legs - control and load sides - must be verified, ideally loaded.

7. B - Control the voltage spike when the coil switches off
   Suppression protects electronics from the inductive kickback when the coil de-energises.

8. B - Watching expected voltage/current feedback on the circuit
   Modules monitor feedback voltage or current and set a fault if it does not match the commanded state.

9. B - Log a circuit fault
   A mismatch between command and feedback triggers diagnostic trouble codes and possibly a fallback.

10. B - No coil current / incorrect feedback when commanded
   The module expects current or a voltage change; an open prevents it and is flagged.




Electrical Pop Quizzes - Answer Key • Quiz 6 - Automotive Relays Explained
Answer Key - Quiz 7 - Vehicle Lighting Technology
Retake date: ________________ Second score: ___ / 10

1. A - High resistance or poor ground on that lamp's circuit
   One dim lamp usually means voltage drop or a poor ground in that branch.

2. B - Make the vehicle more visible during the day
   DRLs improve daytime conspicuity, often at reduced intensity.

3. B - Oils create hot spots that shorten bulb life
   Skin oils cause uneven heating of the quartz envelope and early failure.

4. B - Heating a filament until it glows
   Current heats the filament to incandescence.

5. B - An electric arc through xenon gas and metal salts
   HID uses an arc discharge, requiring a ballast/igniter for high starting voltage.

6. B - Provide high ignition voltage and then regulate lamp current
   The ballast/igniter starts the arc and controls current once lit.

7. B - Low current draw, long life and instant on
   LEDs are efficient, durable and switch instantly, though they need proper drivers and heat management.

8. B - Not light, because LEDs allow current in one direction
   LEDs are diodes, so reverse polarity blocks normal operation.

9. B - Using laser diodes to excite a phosphor that emits white light
   Laser diodes stimulate a phosphor, producing bright white light with safety controls.

10. B - Longer range from a very small, intense light source
   Laser systems achieve long range from a compact source, usually supplementing LED high beam.




Electrical Pop Quizzes - Answer Key • Quiz 7 - Vehicle Lighting Technology
Answer Key - Quiz 8 - Understanding Sensors
Retake date: ________________ Second score: ___ / 10

1. A - Its resistance
   Thermistors change resistance with temperature; most automotive ones are NTC.

2. B - Decreases
   Negative temperature coefficient means resistance falls as temperature rises.

3. A - Changes the resistance of a silicon diaphragm element
   Strain changes the resistance of the sensing element, converted to a signal voltage.

4. A - A varying analogue voltage proportional to pressure
   Pressure changes the bridge output voltage in proportion to pressure.

5. A - Generates a charge/voltage when mechanically stressed
   Piezoelectric materials generate charge under stress, ideal for knock and dynamic events.

6. B - A piezoelectric sensor
   Knock sensors use piezoelectric elements to convert vibration into a voltage signal.

7. B - Capacitance as distance or dielectric changes
   Movement or material change alters capacitance, which electronics convert to a signal.

8. B - Occupant detection, fluid level and touch/proximity sensing
   Capacitance suits non-contact level, occupancy and proximity detection.

9. A - Timing an echo of a high-frequency sound pulse
   Distance is calculated from the time of flight of the reflected ultrasonic pulse.

10. B - False or missed distance warnings
   Contamination blocks or distorts the pulse, causing unreliable detection.




Electrical Pop Quizzes - Answer Key • Quiz 8 - Understanding Sensors
Answer Key - Quiz 9 - Master Control Modules
Retake date: ________________ Second score: ___ / 10

1. C - 5 V
   Equal resistors split the supply equally, giving half at the junction.

2. B - Resistance, changing the signal voltage the module reads
   As sensor resistance changes, the divider ratio and signal voltage change.

3. B - Toward reference voltage, and the sensor/switch pulls it down
   The pull-up holds the line high until the device pulls it toward ground.

4. A - Pulled to ground / low
   A pull-down resistor holds the input low until a device pulls it high.

5. B - Low at all times
   A short to ground overcomes the pull-up and holds the signal low.

6. A - Input - process - output
   Modules read inputs, process them using logic/maps, then command outputs.

7. B - Programming, coding and/or configuration to the vehicle
   Many modules need software, VIN/configuration coding and relearns.

8. B - Multiple unrelated-looking faults and communication errors
   Poor power or ground makes module behaviour erratic and can affect a whole network.

9. A - Programming a module through the diagnostic connector using a pass-through device and manufacturer
software
   A pass-through interface lets a PC and OEM software reprogram modules via the DLC.

10. B - Stable battery voltage maintained with a suitable power supply
   Voltage must stay stable throughout programming or the module can be corrupted.




Electrical Pop Quizzes - Answer Key • Quiz 9 - Master Control Modules
Answer Key - Quiz 10 - Electrical Waveforms Explained
Retake date: ________________ Second score: ___ / 10

1. B - Voltage
   Vertical is voltage (amplitude); horizontal is time.

2. B - Be compressed and lose detail
   A slow time base squeezes cycles together so detail is hidden.

3. B - Capping current to a safe level if a load shorts or overloads
   Limiting protects module drivers from overheating on overload or short.

4. B - Varying the on-time / duty cycle of a fixed-frequency signal
   Changing duty cycle changes average voltage/current delivered to the load.

5. A - A clean square-wave switching between low and high
   Hall sensors switch digitally, giving a square wave.

6. B - An AC sine-like wave whose amplitude and frequency rise with speed
   VR sensors generate AC; faster rotation means higher frequency and amplitude.

7. B - The module's ability to locate crank position / TDC reference
   The gap is the reference; distortion can cause sync and misfire faults.

8. B - Valve timing, sealing and pumping problems from pressure changes
   Pressure traces show compression, power, exhaust and intake events.

9. B - Current is building in the coil primary
   Dwell is coil-on time, building the magnetic field and primary current.

10. B - High secondary resistance such as a wide plug gap or open lead
   High resistance demands higher firing voltage and leaves less energy for spark duration.




Electrical Pop Quizzes - Answer Key • Quiz 10 - Electrical Waveforms Explained
Answer Key - Quiz 11 - Advanced Oscilloscope Techniques
Retake date: ________________ Second score: ___ / 10

1. A - Starter current draw or battery voltage dip as each cylinder comes up on compression
   Each compression stroke loads the starter; a weak cylinder draws less current.

2. B - Cranking with fuelling/ignition disabled as directed
   The engine is cranked without starting so starter load reflects compression.

3. B - That cylinder has lower compression than the others
   Less compression means less starter load, so a smaller current hump.

4. B - Identify which peak belongs to which cylinder
   Sync links each peak in firing order to a specific cylinder.

5. B - How cylinders compare with each other, not absolute pressure
   It is a comparison test; a low cylinder needs follow-up testing for cause and absolute value.

6. A - That the battery and starter circuit are in good condition and fully charged
   A weak battery or starter distorts the pattern and can mimic compression differences.

7. B - A generally weak battery/starter, incorrect cranking speed, or a global engine issue - not one cylinder
   A uniform pattern points to a common cause rather than one cylinder.

8. B - A conventional compression test and/or cylinder leakage test on that cylinder
   Wet/dry compression and leakage testing locate rings, valves or gasket leakage.

9. B - Battery voltage dips as starter load rises on each compression stroke
   Higher starter load pulls battery voltage down, creating a corresponding voltage trace.

10. A - Stop the engine starting and to get a clean, even cranking pattern
   Preventing a start keeps cranking even and safe for comparison.




Electrical Pop Quizzes - Answer Key • Quiz 11 - Advanced Oscilloscope Techniques
Answer Key - Quiz 12 - Testing and Charging Batteries
Retake date: ________________ Second score: ___ / 10

1. B - Dilute sulphuric acid
   Flooded lead-acid cells use sulphuric acid electrolyte covering lead plates.

2. B - 1.265 - 1.280
   Around 1.265-1.280 at reference temperature indicates full charge.

3. B - They require a battery management system to monitor cell voltage, temperature and current
   Lithium chemistry needs BMS protection against overcharge, over-discharge and thermal issues.

4. B - Lower weight and higher energy density
   Lithium packs store more energy per kilogram.

5. B - Battery capacity / cranking ability from its internal conductance
   Conductance testing infers health and CCA capability without a full load test.

6. B - Reasonably charged and terminals are clean and tight
   Testing a discharged or badly connected battery gives misleading failures.

7. B - After modules have gone to sleep, measuring key-off current draw
   Normal sleep current is measured after the vehicle fully powers down.

8. B - Measure voltage drop across fuses or pull fuses one at a time while watching draw fall
   Fuse voltage-drop or sequential fuse removal isolates the draining branch without waking modules where possible.

9. B - Uses multi-stage charging and can adapt rate and mode to battery condition and type
   Smart chargers bulk, absorb and float, and often have AGM/lithium modes and maintenance.

10. B - Undercharge it or damage it if voltage limits are wrong
   Battery type settings matter; AGM and lithium have different voltage limits.




Electrical Pop Quizzes - Answer Key • Quiz 12 - Testing and Charging Batteries
Answer Key - Quiz 13 - Understanding Charging Systems
Retake date: ________________ Second score: ___ / 10

1. A - Spinning a magnetic field inside stationary stator windings
   The rotating rotor field induces AC in the stator, rectified to DC.

2. A - Converts AC from the stator to DC for the vehicle
   Diodes rectify stator AC into usable DC output.

3. B - Controlling rotor field current
   More field current makes a stronger field and higher output.

4. B - A faulty diode or stator winding
   Failed diodes/windings let AC ripple through and reduce output.

5. A - A scope on the output or a meter on AC volts
   A scope pattern or AC voltage measurement reveals abnormal ripple.

6. B - Battery overheating, gassing and damage to electronics
   Overvoltage damages the battery and sensitive electronics.

7. B - Low/intermittent charging, noise and battery warning under load
   The alternator cannot reach required speed/output if the belt slips.

8. B - Checking battery condition, terminals, belt and grounds first
   A weak battery or bad connection mimics alternator failure, so basics come first.

9. C - 13.5 - 14.5 V (system dependent)
   Conventional systems regulate roughly in the mid-13 to mid-14 volt range; smart systems vary.

10. B - High resistance that a voltage-at-battery reading alone can hide
   Loaded drop tests reveal cable and connection resistance between alternator and battery.




Electrical Pop Quizzes - Answer Key • Quiz 13 - Understanding Charging Systems
Answer Key - Quiz 14 - Smart Charging Technology
Retake date: ________________ Second score: ___ / 10

1. B - Match electrical load, battery state, temperature and fuel-economy goals
   Smart control balances charge needs with engine load and emissions/economy targets.

2. B - A fully charged battery needs less, and reducing alternator load saves fuel
   Reducing field when charge is not needed cuts engine drag.

3. B - Recover energy (regenerative-style charging) while engine braking
   Raising output on overrun uses vehicle momentum to recharge the battery.

4. B - Monitor charge/discharge current to calculate battery state
   Current, voltage and temperature data let the module estimate state of charge and health.

5. B - Default to a fixed fallback charging voltage
   Most designs fail-safe to a conventional default voltage so the vehicle stays powered.

6. B - The module may be intentionally commanding a lower voltage at that moment
   Commanded voltage varies; compare scan data, command and battery state before condemning parts.

7. B - Battery state data, commanded/desired voltage, generator feedback and related codes
   Desired vs actual generator data shows whether control or the alternator is at fault.

8. B - Register/reset the battery monitoring system so charging adapts to the new battery
   Battery registration resets learned age/type data; without it charging can be wrong.

9. B - Incorrect charging voltage decisions and warning lights
   Bad inputs lead the module to command inappropriate charging.

10. B - The module to misread or the alternator to undercharge despite a good unit
   Ground resistance affects both output and sensing, mimicking alternator failure.




Electrical Pop Quizzes - Answer Key • Quiz 14 - Smart Charging Technology
Answer Key - Quiz 15 - Mastering Starter Systems
Retake date: ________________ Second score: ___ / 10

1. B - Engage the pinion with the ring gear and close the motor contacts
   The solenoid shifts the pinion into mesh and switches heavy motor current.

2. B - Poor heavy-current contacts, low battery, bad connections or a seized/faulty motor - not the signal alone
   The signal is arriving (click) but heavy current is not turning the motor.

3. A - Magnetic interaction between armature and field windings/coils
   Current in the armature and field creates magnetic forces that rotate the armature.

4. B - Intermittent or no operation and arcing
   Poor brush contact interrupts armature current.

5. B - While cranking, measuring across each cable and connection
   High starter current reveals resistance; drops are measured during cranking.

6. B - Excessive resistance in that cable or its connections
   That drop is far above a healthy cable's small drop under cranking load.

7. B - Kept low - typically under about 0.5 V total in a healthy system (check specifications)
   Excess total drop starves the starter of voltage; always compare with manufacturer specs.

8. B - Frequent restarts and deeper cycling while supporting loads engine-off
   Start-stop duty cycles a normal flooded battery too hard, shortening its life.

9. B - Battery state is low, engine is cold, or a large electrical/HVAC load demands the engine
   Inhibit conditions protect battery, emissions, comfort and safety.

10. B - A starter/battery and management system designed for fast, repeated restarts
   Reinforced starters, suitable batteries and control logic make restarts quick and reliable.




Electrical Pop Quizzes - Answer Key • Quiz 15 - Mastering Starter Systems
Answer Key - Quiz 16 - Modern Vehicle Networks
Retake date: ________________ Second score: ___ / 10

1. B - Body and comfort functions where speed is less critical
   Low-speed CAN suits doors, seats, lighting and other body systems.

2. B - Continue communicating on one wire in some fault conditions
   Fault-tolerant transceivers can operate single-wire in limited faults.

3. B - Differential signals that are mirror images, improving noise immunity
   Differential signalling rejects common-mode noise.

4. B - 60 ohms
   Two 120-ohm terminators in parallel measure about 60 ohms.

5. B - Loss or severe disruption of communication on that bus
   A short collapses differential signalling and modules cannot communicate reliably.

6. B - Deterministic, high-speed, fault-tolerant communication for chassis/safety systems
   FlexRay provides time-determined, redundant communication for critical systems.

7. B - Static time slots in a repeating cycle for guaranteed message timing
   Time-triggered slots guarantee when critical messages are sent.

8. B - Infotainment / multimedia data, often over optical fibre
   MOST carries audio, video and infotainment data around a ring.

9. B - Interrupt the ring and can take down the infotainment network
   A ring break stops data circulating past the break.

10. B - A low-cost single-wire sub-bus where a master controls slave nodes such as switches, motors and sensors
   LIN handles simple body slaves under a master module at low cost.
